Here is a focused 3-week reconditioning block to reintroduce load and movement after a 3-week mild illness with fatigue and 4 kg weight loss. The goal is to restore baseline strength and movement quality safely, reduce injury risk, and set up the client for a full 12-week plan. Given the client is an intermediate lifter with pre-illness numbers: bench 100 kg, squat 140 kg, deadlift 170 kg.

Structure
- Frequency: 4 days per week (upper/lower split) to balance recovery with progressive exposure.
- Focus: gradually reintroduce compound lifts at submaximal loads, emphasize technique, add essential accessories for mobility, core, and return-to-sport conditioning. Weekly progression via load and/or volume conservatively.
- RPE target: RPE 6-7 on main lifts in weeks 1-2, aiming toward RPE 7-8 by week 3 with careful planful progression.
- Recovery emphasis: start with 7–9 hours sleep, prioritize protein intake ~1.6–2.2 g/kg/day, hydration, and basic deload-like pacing within weeks if needed.

Assumptions
- No contraindications; client can train 4 days/week with adequate recovery.
- Equipment available: barbell, plates, squat rack, bench, dumbbells, machines for accessories, proper footwear, and safety gear.

Week-by-week plan overview
- Week 1: Reintroduction with low-to-moderate volume, establish technique, minimize fatigue. Main lifts at ~60-65% of 1RM (bench, squat, deadlift), 3–4 sets of 5–6 reps. Accessory work focused on upper back, glutes, hips, core.
- Week 2: Gradual volume and slight load increase to ~65-70% 1RM for main lifts. Begin light sets of 5 with a couple of heavier work sets but still controlled. Maintain technique emphasis.
- Week 3: Build toward baseline exposure with closer-to-pre-illness loads but still conservative. Main lifts at ~70-75% 1RM for 3–4 sets of 4–5 reps, plus a low-volume accessory block to support technique and mobility. Anticipate feeling closer to baseline by week’s end.

Detailed plan

Weekly structure (4 days)
- Day A: Upper body (pressing emphasis)
- Day B: Lower body (squat/deadlift emphasis)
- Day C: Upper body (pulling emphasis)
- Day D: Lower body (hinge/accessory emphasis)

Week 1
- Main lifts: all at 60–65% of estimated 1RM (use conservative estimates based on pre-illness numbers; adjust down if needed)
  - Bench Press: 4 sets x 5 reps at 60–65% 1RM
  - Back Squat: 4 sets x 5 reps at 60–65% 1RM
  - Deadlift (from floor or as Romanian deadlift if fatigue): 3 sets x 5 reps at 60–65% 1RM
- Accessory emphasis (2–3 per session, 2–3 sets each)
  - Upper body days: 
    - Dumbbell incline or flat bench accessory: 3x8–12
    - Barbell/DB rows or Pendlay rows: 3x8–12
    - Face pulls or band pull-aparts: 3x15
    - Lateral raises: 2–3x12
  - Lower body days:
    - Hip thrusts or glute bridges: 3x8–12
    - Romanian deadlifts or eccentric deadlift work: 3x8
    - Lunges or split squats: 3x8 per leg
    - Core work: planks or Pallof presses: 3x30–45s
- Conditioning/energy systems: optional 10–15 minutes of light cardio after sessions or on off days (easy pace, RPE 3–4)
- Mobility: 5–10 minutes daily focusing on hips, thoracic spine, shoulders; 2–3 dedicated mobility sessions per week

Week 2
- Main lifts: 65–70% 1RM
  - Bench Press: 4 sets x 5 reps at 65–70%
  - Back Squat: 4 sets x 5 reps at 65–70%
  - Deadlift: 3 sets x 5 reps at 65–70% (consider paused or conventional depending on comfort)
- Accessories: maintain variety, slight progression
  - Upper body days:
    - DB or barbell rows: 3x8–12
    - Push-ups or DB floor press: 3x8–12
    - Face pulls: 3x12–15
    - Bicep curls or triceps accessory: 2–3x10–12
  - Lower body days:
    - Hip thrusts: 3x8–12
    - Romanian deadlifts: 3x6–8
    - Step-ups or split squats: 3x8 per leg
    - Core: weighted carries or anti-rotation: 3x20–30s
- RPE target: stay around 7 on main lifts; adjust if fatigue high
- Sleep and nutrition: reinforce protein intake and hydration

Week 3
- Main lifts: 70–75% 1RM, push toward closer to baseline
  - Bench Press: 4 sets x 4–5 reps at 70–75% (or 4 sets x 5 at 70% if form requires)
  - Back Squat: 4 sets x 4–5 reps at 70–75%
  - Deadlift: 3 sets x 4–5 reps at 70–75%
- Accessory emphasis: maintain quality, reduce total volume slightly if needed to stay fresh
  - Upper body:
    - Rows or weighted pull-ups: 3x6–8
    - incline press or DB bench: 3x6–8
    - Face pulls: 3x12–15
    - Core: 2–3 sets of 60s side planks or anti-extension work
  - Lower body:
    - Front squats or tempo squats (if comfortable): 3x4–6
    - Glute bridges or hip thrusts: 3x8–10
    - Hamstring curls or face-down machine hip extensions: 3x10–12
    - Calves: 2x12–15
- Weekly check-in: assess readiness to ramp toward higher loads; any persistent fatigue or symptoms should guide further adjustment
- Conditioning: minimal but present; consider 1 light conditioning session (20 minutes) if energy allows

Training cues and technique notes
- Warm-up: 8–12 minutes general, plus 5–10 minutes specific warm-up for main lifts (progressive loads, ramp sets, mobility)
- Bench: ensure scapular retraction and slight tuck; keep feet planted; bar path vertical
- Squat: bracing with tight core, chest up, hips back; depth consistent with mobility
- Deadlift: maintain neutral spine; hip hinge; pull from mid-foot; consider switching to RDL or lighter loads if fatigue
- Tempo: for weeks 2–3, consider a controlled tempo (2 seconds down, 1 second up) for at least one heavier set per lift to emphasize control
- Volume management: if fatigue accumulates, reduce one accessory set per exercise or swap to lower impact movements (e.g., DB rows instead of Pendlay for a session)

Nutrition and recovery components
- Protein: target 1.6–2.2 g/kg/day; distribute evenly across 3–4 meals
- Calories: start with maintenance or a modest surplus if weight regain is a priority; monitor weight and adjust by 200–300 kcal per week as needed
- Hydration: aim for 30–40 ml/kg/day depending on activity levels
- Sleep: target 7–9 hours per night; limit screen time before bed; consider a short nap if fatigue persists
- Recovery practices: light mobility work daily, 5–10 minutes post-workout; consider gentle yoga or walking on off days
- Illness recovery markers: if fatigue persists beyond week 2 or symptoms worsen (fever, chest tightness, deep fatigue), pause intensity and revert to very light circuits focusing on technique and movement quality; consult healthcare if persistent

Progression plan post-3 weeks
- If tolerating well, advance to a more formal 4-week progression into Week 4 with main lifts at roughly 75–80% 1RM, gradually adding volume or decreasing rest to rebuild baseline performance
- Transition toward a normalized 3–4 day upper/lower split with linear or small-step progression, incorporating more targeted volume per lift as fitness returns

Notes for implementation
- Use objective checks at the end of Week 3 to compare to pre-illness benchmarks. If possible, do non-fatiguing 1RM attempts or rep max tests to calibrate Week 4 load targets, but only if energy and form permit.
- Safety: ensure good equipment setup, warm-up properly, and avoid any pain-limiting movements. If pain or unusual symptoms appear, scale back and consult a clinician.
- Communication: check in on fatigue levels daily; adjust plans if the client reports persistent fatigue, sleep issues, or appetite changes.

If you want, I can tailor the exact set/rep prescriptions to the client’s exact 1RM estimates or adjust based on available equipment (e.g., if you have a dedicated power rack, machines, or limited benches).

Here is a specific week-1 load prescription you can use, based on the client’s pre-illness 1RM figures and the goal to reintroduce load safely.

Assumptions and approach
- Pre-illness 1RM: bench 100 kg, squat 140 kg, deadlift 170 kg
- Week 1 target intensity: roughly 60–65% of pre-illness 1RM for main lifts, with emphasis on technique, control, and recovery
- Use conservative estimates to account for fatigue, possible lingering fatigue, and reduced training tolerance
- If technique or fatigue suggests, reduce further by 5–10% and/or drop a set

Calculated working numbers for Week 1
- Bench press: 4 sets x 5 reps at 60–65% of 100 kg
  - 60%: 60 kg
  - 65%: 65 kg
  Target range: 60–65 kg
  Recommended target: 4x5 at 62.5 kg (you can round to 60 or 65 kg depending on bar feel)
  Practical prescription: 4 sets x 5 reps at 60–62.5 kg (e.g., 60 kg if you want a clean re-acclimation)

- Back squat: 4 sets x 5 reps at 60–65% of 140 kg
  - 60%: 84 kg
  - 65%: 91 kg
  Target range: 84–91 kg
  Recommended target: 4x5 at 85 kg (round to nearest 5 kg)
  Practical prescription: 4 sets x 5 reps at 85 kg

- Deadlift: 3 sets x 5 reps at 60–65% of 170 kg
  - 60%: 102 kg
  - 65%: 110.5 kg
  Target range: 102–110 kg
  Recommended target: 3x5 at 105 kg (midpoint) or 110 kg if feel is good and technique is solid
  Practical prescription: 3 sets x 5 reps at 105 kg (or 110 kg if confident)

Notes for execution
- Warm-up: ramp to working weights with 2–3 progressive sets per lift (e.g., 40–50% for 5 reps, 60% for 3 reps, then work sets)
- Technique checks: ensure bracing, bar path, and full range of motion with no grinding
- RPE target: aim for RPE 6–7 on each working set (moderate effort, no grind)
- Rest: 2–3 minutes between main lift sets
- Adjustments: if any lift feels off (form breakdown, fatigue), drop 5–10% for the set or reduce to 3x5 at the lower end
- Accessories: follow the plan as previously outlined, but keep volume reasonable to support recovery (2–3 sets per accessory)

If you have to adjust due to equipment or specific fatigue signals, here are safe alternative targets within the same week-1 framework:
- Bench: 4x5 at 58–60 kg if technique or fatigue is a concern
- Squat: 4x5 at 80–85 kg if you’re cautious about knee/hip tolerance
- Deadlift: 3x5 at 100–105 kg if you’re cautious about fatigue or grip

Great—let’s reintroduce cardio at a level that supports recovery and return to his prior 10k/week volume without undermining strength work.

Assumptions
- Pre-illness cardio: ~10k/week total, likely spread across 2–3 days
- Post-illness: fatigue present, 4 kg weight loss; we’ll reintroduce cardio gradually and keep sessions easy to moderate to prioritize recovery and appetite
- Goal: regain 10k/week progressively over Weeks 1–3 while preserving strength work

Cardio structure for Week 1
- Total cardio target: ~20–25 minutes of easy-to-moderate cardio per week, added to 2–3 days, plus optional light active recovery on off days
- Intensity: RPE 3–5 (conversational pace), zone based on perceived effort rather than max HR
- Modes: low-impact options preferred on recovery days (elliptical, cycling, brisk walking, job-specific incline walks)

Suggested distribution
- Day after lower body or on a rest day, choose one:
  - Option A: 2 sessions of 12–15 minutes each (total ~24–30 minutes)
  - Option B: 1 longer session of 20–25 minutes
- Frequency: 2 cardio sessions this week, plus optional light movement on lifting days post-workout (5–10 minutes, easy)

Week 1 cardio prescription (two options; choose one)
Option A (2 shorter sessions)
- Session 1: 12 minutes easy cycling or brisk walk (RPE 3–4)
- Session 2: 12–15 minutes easy elliptical or incline treadmill walk (RPE 3–4)

Option B (one longer session)
- Session: 20–25 minutes easy jog or brisk walk (RPE 4)

Notes
- Do cardio on non-lift days if possible to maximize recovery; if you must, perform after lifting at very low intensity or as a separate short session.
- Monitor appetite, sleep, and fatigue. If energy drops or sleep quality declines, back off cardio load by 5–10 minutes or swap to 1 lighter session.
- Hydration and fueling: ensure adequate fueling around cardio (a small carb/protein snack pre- or post sessions if appetite allows, especially given recent weight loss).
- Progression across Weeks 1–3: aim to increase cardio volume by ~5–10 minutes per week, or add one extra day of 10–15 minutes, while keeping RPE under 5. If symptoms of overreaching appear (persistent fatigue, sleep disruption, mood changes), maintain or reduce.

Integrating with Week 1 lifting plan
- Main lifts remain the priority; cardio should not excessively tax recovery.
- If you’re stacking both cardio and heavy lifting in a single day, place cardio after the lifting session or on a separate day, and keep it light.
- Example weekly layout (one possible structure):
  - Mon: Lift A (bench) + 12–15 min cardio (optional after lift)
  - Tue: Cardio 12–15 min
  - Thu: Lift B (squat) + 12–15 min cardio (optional after lift)
  - Sat: Lift C (deadlift) + optional 12–15 min cardio
  - Wed/Fri/Sun: light movement, mobility, or complete rest as needed

If you’d like, I can tailor the exact cardio modality and duration to his preference (e.g., cycling vs. running) and fit it precisely around the 4-day lift schedule you’re using.

Here’s a practical nutrition framework for the 3-week reconditioning block, designed to support weight regain, training recovery, and return to baseline strength.

Goals
- Rebuild lean mass and restore body weight toward pre-illness levels
- Support training performance and recovery with adequate protein and calories
- Minimize fat gain while restoring energy availability

Estimated targets (based on a 41-year-old male, intermediate lifter)
- Body weight: assume approximately 4 kg down from baseline; goal is to regain toward baseline over 3 weeks, depending on appetite and adherence
- Protein: 1.6–2.2 g per kg of body weight per day
  - If he weighs around 85–90 kg during reconditioning, target protein ~136–198 g/day
- Calories: start near maintenance or a modest surplus
  - Maintenance estimate for a moderately active adult male around this size ~ 2,400–2,800 kcal/day (adjust for activity level and body comp)
  - Start with a small surplus of +200–300 kcal/day if appetite allows, aiming to regain weight gradually
  - If appetite is very low, prioritize protein and settle calories near maintenance, then reassess after Week 1
- Carbohydrates: support training energy, ~3–5 g/kg/day depending on volume
  - For 85–90 kg, this is roughly 255–450 g/day
- Fats: remaining calories, typically 0.8–1.0 g/kg/day as a baseline
  - For 85–90 kg, ~70–90 g/day

Meal timing and distribution
- Protein distribution: aim for 0.32–0.5 g/kg per meal across 4–6 meals to maximize muscle protein synthesis
  - Example: 25–40 g protein per meal
- Pre- and post-workout nutrition:
  - Pre-workout: a balanced meal or snack 1.5–2 hours before lifting (protein + carbs, moderate fat)
  - Post-workout: 0.3–0.6 g/kg carbohydrate with 0.3–0.4 g/kg protein within 2 hours of training
- Sleep nutrition: a small protein-rich snack before bed can help with overnight recovery
  - Example: 20–30 g casein or yogurt with a small portion of fruit

Food strategy and choices
- Prioritize whole foods: lean proteins (chicken, turkey, fish, lean beef, eggs), dairy, legumes, tofu, whole grains, fruits, vegetables, healthy fats (olive oil, nuts, seeds, avocado)
- Liquid calories: use shakes or smoothies to boost intake if appetite is low (e.g., protein shake with banana, oats, peanut butter)
- Appetite management: multiple smaller meals if larger meals feel heavy; include high-volume, nutrient-dense options (vegetables, fruits) to support micronutrient intake
- Hydration: aim for 2.5–3.5 liters/day (adjust for sweating and training)

Monitoring and adjustment
- Weekly check-ins: track weight, appetite, sleep quality, and training performance
- If weight loss continues after Week 1, increase daily calories by 150–250 kcal and reassess in Week 2
- If fatigue or digestion becomes an issue, adjust macronutrient balance (slightly higher carbs on training days, moderate fat on rest days) and ensure protein targets are met
- If weight returns toward baseline and appetite improves, continue the maintenance-surplus approach for Week 2–3, then reassess for the transition to a full 12-week program

Practical daily template (example for 85–90 kg athlete)
- Breakfast: 25–35 g protein, 60–80 g carbs, fats 15–25 g
- Snack: 25–40 g protein, 30–60 g carbs
- Lunch: 30–40 g protein, 70–100 g carbs, fats 15–25 g
- Pre-workout: 20–40 g carbs + 15–25 g protein
- Post-workout: 30–50 g carbs + 25–40 g protein
- Dinner: 25–40 g protein, 40–60 g carbs, fats 15–25 g
- Optional evening snack: 20–30 g protein (casein or Greek yogurt)

Red flags and when to adjust
- If fat gain is rapid and appetite remains high: persist with maintenance calories for a week, then reintroduce a small surplus
- If energy is consistently low or sleep is disrupted: ease back calories slightly, emphasize protein, and consider increasing fibrous carbs and fluids
- If digestion is unsettled: spread protein more evenly, reduce very large meals, and ensure fiber and hydration are balanced

If you’d like, I can tailor these numbers precisely to the client’s current weight, activity level, and preferences, and provide a day-by-day meal plan aligned with the 4-day training split.

Short answer: likely not reasonable to jump straight to pre-illness loads after 3 weeks off with fatigue and a 4 kg weight loss. Lounging on a “feels fine today” signal can be deceptive when returning from illness. Here’s a clear framework to decide and a safe path forward.

Key considerations
- Residual fatigue and recent illness: Even if energy feels normal today, the body may still be in recovery mode. Immune and muscular systems can lag behind feel-good days.
- Weight loss and appetite dynamics: A 4 kg drop suggests energy deficit. Reintroducing heavy loading before restoring energy availability can blunt appetite, impair recovery, or increase soreness/injury risk.
- Training tolerance and technique risk: After time off, especially with a back-to-basics reconditioning phase, you want to re-establish technique and tendon–bone loading in a controlled progression to minimize form breakdown and injuries (knees, lumbar spine, shoulders).
- Autoregulation is prudent: Use objective signs (not just mood) to gauge readiness: quality of movement, form, soreness, sleep, and daily energy, not only “today I feel good.”

What a safer decision framework looks like
Option A: Conservative re-entry (recommended)
- Start Week 1 as planned with 60–65% of pre-illness 1RM for main lifts.
- Treat Week 1 as a deliberate re-entry: permit 4x5 at 60–62.5 kg bench, 4x5 at 85 kg squat, 3x5 at 105 kg deadlift (midpoints or lower end if form or fatigue shows).
- Use Week 1 to re-establish technique, ramp up blood flow, and assess readiness to progress.
- If any lift or movement shows form breakdown, reduce load by 5–10% or reduce sets from 4 to 3 for that lift.
- Keep Week 1 cardio light and accumulation-friendly (as previously planned).

Option B: Very cautious scaled re-entry (if self-monitoring flags appear)
- Use a “deload-like” first week but still with lighter loads, e.g., 50–55% of pre-illness 1RM for 3x5 across main lifts.
- Keep main lifts in a technique-forward zone, with longer rest (2:30–3:30) and strict control.
- Add only minimal accessories in Week 1 (or shift to bodyweight orTRX-based drills) to rebuild movement tolerance.

What could justify jumping to pre-illness loads?
- Objective multi-day stability: perfect sleep 7–9h, appetite robust, no lingering symptoms (fever, chest symptoms, GI upset), morning HR stable and non-elevated, resting heart rate not elevated vs baseline.
- Objective performance checks: controlled technique, no pain with light warm-ups, and ability to complete 3–4 sets with proper form at near baseline loads without excessive fatigue.
- If you have a recent test (e.g., a non-fatiguing movement screen and good squat depth without pain, a clean 2–3 ramp sets at 30–40% and a few singles at 60–70% with zero deviation), you could consider moving into Week 2 intensity by the end of Week 1—but not the full pre-illness loads for Week 1.

Practical plan if you proceed with Week 1 as planned
- Session structure remains 4 days/week (upper/lower split) with main lifts at 60–65%.
- Use precise load targets:
  - Bench: 4x5 at 60–62.5 kg (as estimated)
  - Back squat: 4x5 at 85 kg
  - Deadlift: 3x5 at 105 kg
- Monitor daily indicators:
  - Sleep quality and duration
  - Appetite and GI comfort
  - Perceived recovery 0–10 scale (increase in soreness, stiffness)
  - Performance quality on warm-ups and first working set (any red flags)
- Post-workout checks: ensure you’re not dragging feet or grinding, adjust immediately if needed.
- Cardio: keep to 20–25 minutes total for Week 1, easy intensity, to support appetite and recovery.

What to do if Week 1 feels tougher than expected
- If any main lift moves into 7–8 RPE range on sets, or form degrades, drop to 3x5 at the lower bound (e.g., bench 60 kg, squat 80–85 kg, deadlift 95–100 kg) and keep volume consistent.
- Consider replacing one main lift with a lighter alternative (e.g., switch to paused bench or lighter tempo squats) to maintain movement patterns without overloading joints.
- Emphasize nutrition and sleep; if appetite remains limited or weight still trending down after Week 1, adjust calories upward modestly (increment 150–200 kcal/day) and reassess.

Bottom line
- It’s safer and more sustainable to begin Week 1 at reduced loads (60–65% of pre-illness 1RM) even if today feels fine, then escalate selectively into Week 2 based on objective recovery signals. Jumping straight to pre-illness loads risks poor technique, higher fatigue, and potential injury. If you want, I can tailor exact week-1 loads to the client’s current weight, energy, and any recent test results, and provide a day-by-day plan with contingencies.

Great question. Readiness for full-intensity work isn’t a single metric—it’s a constellation of signals from sleep, appetite, performance, and how the body feels. Use a blunt, practical checklist over a 1–2 week window to decide whether to proceed or pull back. Here are the main signals and how to interpret them.

Key readiness signals (positive indicators)
- Sleep: 7–9 hours per night, consistent quality, no frequent awakenings; morning restlessness absent.
- Appetite and weight: steady or returning appetite; weight stabilizing or trending back toward pre-illness baseline within 1–2 weeks.
- Resting metrics: resting heart rate (RHR) near baseline or showing no persistent elevation (e.g., +0 to +3 beats/min above pre-illness baseline) when measured first thing in the morning.
- Training tolerance in-week: warm-ups feel smooth, no unusual aches, joints feel stable, and first working sets can be completed with RPE around 6–7 without form breaks.
- Recovery markers: minimal muscle soreness that dissipates within 24–48 hours, no persistent fatigue after workouts, and ability to perform planned volume without grinding.
- Performance signals: training numbers (speed, bar speed, or approximate reps in reserve) return toward pre-illness levels across back-to-back sessions.

Key signals that suggest you’re not ready for full intensity
- Sleep disruption or poor quality for several consecutive nights; consistently high fatigue.
- Persistent fatigue or malaise after workouts beyond 24–48 hours.
- Appetite suppression or ongoing weight loss without intentional plan to regain it.
- Resting heart rate elevated by more than 5–10 bpm above baseline for several days, or HRV flags if you track it.
- Pain, joint pain, or movement-driven soreness that worsens with load; technique breaks (poor bracing, form drift) on main lifts.
- Inability to complete planned sets/reps at target intensities due to fatigue or technique breakdown (e.g., 2–3 sets in and form starts to degrade).

Objective signals and practical checks
- 2-week window rule: if you see two or more positive readiness signals consistently (sleep, appetite, HR, and ability to complete planned sets at target loading with good technique), consider progressing intensity in Week 2 or Week 3.
- Objective tests (optional, quick and low risk):
  - Submaximal ramp test: perform 2–3 ramp sets on each main lift at light-to-moderate intensities and compare bar velocity or reps could be used if you have a coach’s eye or velocity measurer.
  - 1–2 non-fatiguing movement screens: overhead squat, hip hinge pattern, and single-leg balance tests to ensure mechanics are stable without pain.
  - 1–2 practice sets at moderate intensity (e.g., 75% 1RM for 3–4 reps) on a workout day and see if technique and bar speed feel controlled and pain-free.

Decision framework for progression
- If 6–7 on RP scale and all signals favorable: you can progress toward higher intensity in Week 2 or 3, increasing main lift intensity by ~5–10% and/or adding 1 more working set if recovery remains solid.
- If mixed signals (some positives, some concerns): hold intensity steady for another week, perhaps adding one easy accessory block or replacing one main lift with a technique-focused variation (paused reps, tempo work) to rebuild tolerance.
- If adverse signals dominate (pain, sleep disruption, significant fatigue): pull back to a light deload week, minimize lower-body loading, emphasize mobility and technique, and revisit readiness in 7–10 days.

Practical monitoring plan
- Daily checks: sleep (hours/quality), appetite, mood, and fatigue level (0–10 scale).
- Morning metrics (few days per week): resting heart rate, and if available, HRV.
- After each session: rate perceived exertion on main lifts and note any technique issues or pain.
- Weekly review: compare weights lifted, reps completed, bar speed (if tracked), and subjective readiness. If week-to-week progress stalls or regressions occur, reassess.

Communication and safety
- If symptoms return (fever, chest pain, shortness of breath), pause training and seek medical guidance.
- Always prioritize technique over loading. If form begins to break, back off immediately even if signals look favorable.
- Plan for a flexible timeline: readiness for full intensity may take longer for some clients after illness; have a clear path to progress or regress depending on how signals evolve.

If you’d like, I can tailor a concrete readiness checklist with your client’s exact metrics (baseline 1RM, recent HR, sleep hours, appetite changes) and propose a staged progression plan with specific load targets for Weeks 2–4.

Great idea. Scheduling a non-fatiguing 1RM test in the back half of Week 3 gives you objective baselines to reset the subsequent program. Here’s a practical, safety-focused approach that minimizes risk while still giving you clean data.

Overall approach
- Timing: 1RM tests for bench, squat, and deadlift on Week 3 Day 4 or Week 3 last training session, after completing main lifts that day (not after a max-effort session that would spike fatigue the same day).
- Structure: use standardized attempts with ample warm-up, clear target progression, and strict form. Do not attempt all three lifts to max on the same day if fatigue is a concern; consider testing two lifts on one day and the third on a separate day within Week 3, while maintaining good recovery between tests.
- Safety: ensure proper setup, a spotter or safety equipment, and a plan to abort if technique deteriorates or pain arises.

Proposed Week 3 plan with 1RM testing
- Week 3 overview: main lifts at 70–75% 1RM with lower volume to taper fatigue, plus a final day reserved for 1RM testing. Use the same split you’re using (e.g., Day A: bench, Day B: squat, Day C: deadlift, Day D: optional accessory/conditioning).
- Day structure for testing (example across lifts; adjust to your preferred order):
  - Bench 1RM testing: 
    - Warm-up: 5–10 minutes mobility + 4–5 ramp sets: e.g., as you approach working sets: 40% x5, 50% x3, 60% x3, 70% x2, 80% x1, then attempts at 85%, 90%, 95% if clean.
    - Attempt progression: up to 95% then attempt 1RM attempts in 1–2 kg steps to find max with solid technique.
  - Squat 1RM testing (could be on a separate day to avoid cumulative fatigue):
    - Warm-up: ramp sets with emphasis on bracing and depth, starting around 40–50% and working to 80–85% before single attempts.
    - Attempt progression: 90%, 95%, then 100%+ with small jumps, only if prior attempts are clean.
  - Deadlift 1RM testing (same day or separate day):
    - Warm-up focusing on hinge pattern and grip; ramp to 100% and attempt.
- Volume/feels: keep volume in the week modest; avoid heavy accessory work the same day as your 1RM attempts to reduce fatigue risk.

A concrete, safe testing sequence (example)
- Week 3 Day 1: Bench main work + light accessories
  - 4x5 at 60–65% (as previously planned)
  - Accessory blocks
- Week 3 Day 3: Squat main work + light accessories
  - 4x5 at 70–75%
  - Accessory blocks
- Week 3 Day 5: 1RM testing for bench or deadlift (rotate)
  - Bench 1RM attempt session (if you test bench first, allow 3–5 minutes between attempts; otherwise separate the days)
  - After bench test, rest and then schedule Deadlift test on a separate day or later in the week
- Week 3 Day 6 or Week 3 Day 7: Deadlift 1RM attempt session
  - Similar warm-up and progressive attempts
- Optional: if fatigue is high, you can push the 1RM tests back one week or split into 2 days with 3–5 days recovery in between.

Guidelines to protect the client
- Controller: use a strict stopping rule (if form breaks or pain arises, abort the attempt and move to the previous safe load).
- Tape and safety: ensure proper spotters or racks with safety pins; use lifting belts as needed for heavy singles.
- Rest between attempts: 3–5 minutes for heavy singles; longer if needed to recover technique and bar speed.
- Neutral tempo and bracing: emphasize proper bracing, hip hinge, and bar path on all attempts.
- Nutrition and recovery: ensure adequate protein and carbs in the meals around test days; prioritize sleep to support nervous system recovery.

Post-1RM plan
- Once you have the new 1RM numbers, reset your program:
  - Recalculate weekly intensities based on the new 1RM, adjusting volume and sets/reps accordingly.
  - Consider a brief reconditioning ramp again if the client shows signs of fatigue after the test.
  - Build a new 12-week plan from Week 1 of the new phase using more precise load targets (e.g., 72–78% for initial blocks, then progress).

Communication and contingency
- If the client’s energy or technique flags during testing, switch to safer submaximal targets (e.g., 5–3–2 rep max approach) and postpone the max attempts until readiness is solid.
- Document all results carefully (attempt weights, reps achieved, form notes, any pain or tightness).

If you’d like, I can generate a day-by-day Week 3 testing protocol tailored to your client’s exact schedule (which days you’re planning for Week 3, whether you want to test bench first or rotate lifts, and how you’ll space rest days). I can also convert the new 1RM results into a concrete Week 4 onward plan with conservative progression to full intensity.

Here is the integrated 3-week reconditioning block with all adjustments discussed. It’s structured for a 4-day upper/lower split, reintroducing load safely after 3 weeks off with fatigue and weight loss, and including cardio, nutrition framing, readiness signals, and a planned Week 3 1RM testing window. Pre-illness 1RM: bench 100 kg, squat 140 kg, deadlift 170 kg.

Overall goals
- Safely recondition back toward baseline strength with technique emphasis, while rebuilding energy availability, appetite, and body weight.
- Reintroduce cardio to return to ~10k/week volume (in week-by-week progression) without compromising strength recovery.
- Establish objective baselines via Week 3 1RM tests to reset the program.

Weekly structure (4 days)
- Day A: Upper body press emphasis
- Day B: Lower body squat emphasis
- Day C: Upper body pull emphasis
- Day D: Lower body hinge/accessory emphasis

Week 1 (reintroduction, load and technique focus)
Main lifts (subset of Week 1 targets; conservative, technique-first)
- Bench press: 4 sets x 5 reps at 60–62.5% of pre-illness 1RM (target 60–65 kg; use 60 kg if needed for form)
- Back squat: 4 sets x 5 reps at 85 kg (60–65% of 140 kg; approximate; adjust to keep 60–62.5% feel)
- Deadlift: 3 sets x 5 reps at 105 kg (60–65% of 170 kg)

Rationale and notes
- This week prioritizes technique, full range, and recovery. If any lift shows form drift, reduce by 5–10% or drop a set.
- Warm-ups: 8–12 minutes general, plus 3–4 ramp sets per lift (e.g., 40–50%, 60%, 70%, then work sets).
- Rest: 2–3 minutes between main sets.

Accessory blocks (2–3 per session, 2–3 sets each)
- Upper body days:
  - DB incline or flat bench accessory: 3x8–12
  - Rows or Pendlay rows: 3x8–12
  - Face pulls or band pull-aparts: 3x15
  - Lateral raises: 2–3x12
- Lower body days:
  - Hip thrusts or glute bridges: 3x8–12
  - Romanian deadlifts or eccentric deadlift work: 3x8
  - Lunges or split squats: 3x8 per leg
  - Core (planks or Pallof presses): 3x30–45s

Cardio (introduce easy volume)
- Total cardio target: ~20–25 minutes for the week, easy to moderate (RPE 3–5)
- Distribution: 2 sessions (2x12–15 minutes or 1x20–25 minutes), optional light movement on lifting days post-workout
- Modes: cycling, walking, elliptical, incline treadmill; avoid maximal efforts

Mobility and recovery
- Daily 5–10 minutes focused on hips, thoracic spine, shoulders
- 2–3 dedicated mobility sessions per week
- Sleep target: 7–9 hours; protein intake ~1.6–2.2 g/kg/day; hydration

Nutrition targets (week 1 focus; see Week 1–3 plan for progression)
- Protein: ~1.6–2.2 g/kg/day
- Calories: maintenance to modest surplus, about +200–300 kcal/day if appetite allows
- Carbs: ~3–5 g/kg/day to support training energy
- Fats: remainder of calories, roughly 0.8–1.0 g/kg/day
- Meal distribution: 4–6 meals with 25–40 g protein per meal
- Hydration: 2.5–3.5 L/day

Readiness signals and autoregulation
- Daily checks: sleep quality, appetite, mood, fatigue (0–10)
- Morning metrics: resting HR (compared to baseline; aim for near baseline or only +0 to +3 bpm)
- In-session: main lift RPE around 6–7 on work sets; no technique degradation
- If multiple signals point toward fatigue, scale back intensity and/or volume for the following week

Week 2 (gradual progression, closer to baseline exposure)
Main lifts (slightly higher tolerance and load)
- Bench press: 4 sets x 5 reps at 65–70% 1RM (target ~65–70% of pre-illness; e.g., 65–70 kg)
- Back squat: 4 sets x 5 reps at 65–70% 1RM (target ~90–95 kg)
- Deadlift: 3 sets x 5 reps at 65–70% 1RM (target ~110–115 kg)

Rationale
- Slight load increase from Week 1 while maintaining 5-rep sets to preserve technique and recovery. Use RPE ~7 on main lifts.

Accessory blocks (progressively increasing)
- Upper body days:
  - Rows/Pulls: 3x8–12
  - Push variations: 3x8–12 (incline DB or floor press)
  - Face pulls: 3x12–15
  - Curls/Triceps: 2–3x10–12
- Lower body days:
  - Hip thrusts/glute bridges: 3x8–12
  - Romanian deadlifts: 3x6–8
  - Split squats or step-ups: 3x8 per leg
  - Core: 3x20–30s carries or anti-rotation

Cardio progression
- Total cardio target: ~25–35 minutes for the week
- Distribution: 2–3 sessions; aim to add 5–10 minutes compared to Week 1
- Intensity: maintain RPE 3–5; consider one optional light tempo day (shorter, slightly faster but still conversational pace)

Nutrition progression
- Reassess weight: aim to regain some weight toward baseline
- Maintain protein: 1.6–2.2 g/kg/day
- Calorie target: maintain +150–300 kcal/day if appetite is good; favor a slight surplus if weight remains below baseline
- Carbs: adjust to energy needs; keep training fuel high
- Hydration: 2.5–3.5 L/day

Week 3 (optimize readiness for full intensity and plan 1RM testing)
Main lifts (70–75% of baseline 1RM range; conservative but building toward baseline)
- Bench press: 4 sets x 4–5 reps at 70–75% 1RM
- Back squat: 4 sets x 4–5 reps at 70–75% 1RM
- Deadlift: 3 sets x 4–5 reps at 70–75% 1RM

1RM testing window (late Week 3)
- Plan to test bench, squat, and deadlift as a safe, non-fatiguing sequence. Recommendations:
  - Week 3 Day 4 or 3–4: bench 1RM attempts (rotate with other lifts to manage fatigue)
  - Week 3 Day 5 or 6: squat 1RM attempts
  - Week 3 Day 7: deadlift 1RM attempts
- Testing structure per lift:
  - 5–10 min warm-up ramp to working sets
  - Gradual increases: 40%, 50%, 60%, 70%, 80%, 85%, 90%, 95%, then 1RM attempts with 1–2 kg increments if form remains solid
  - Allow 3–5 minutes between attempts; ensure proper form and safe execution
- If fatigue or form breaks, stop attempts and use a lower-load maximum (e.g., 5–3–2 rep max approach) and postpone final 1RM attempts to a later date

Post-1RM plan (Week 4 onward)
- Recalculate 1RM targets based on test results
- Reset the weekly progression:
  - Example starting range: 72–78% 1RM for initial volume blocks
  - Progressive intakes: aim for steady progression with micro-load increases weekly
- If fatigue after testing, implement a brief maintenance or delayed progression block before increasing again

Daily schedule example (one possible weekly layout)
- Monday: Day A – Upper body press
  - Bench 4x5 @ 60–62.5% (Week 1) → advance to 65–70% by Week 2; 70–75% by Week 3
  - Accessory blocks
  - Optional cardio after lifting (low intensity)
- Tuesday: Day B – Lower body squat
  - Squat 4x5 @ 85 kg (Week 1) → 90–95 kg Week 2 → 95–100 kg Week 3
  - Accessory blocks
- Thursday: Day C – Upper body pull
  - Rows/pull variations; accessory work
  - Cardio optional after
- Friday: Day D – Lower body hinge/accessory
  - Deadlift 3x5 @ 105 kg (Week 1) → 110–115 kg Week 2 → 115–120 kg Week 3
  - Core and mobility

Strict caveats and safety
- If any red flags appear (pain, chest tightness, fever, persistent cough, dizziness), pause and reassess with a medical professional if needed.
- Technique first: always prioritize form; if form breaks, reduce load or volume immediately.
- Use a proper warm-up and ramp protocol for each lift; ensure appropriate safety equipment and a spotter as needed.
- Hydration and nutrition should support the increased training demand, especially around Week 3 testing.

Notes and customization
- If you want, I can tailor exact day-by-day load targets to the client’s current weight during Week 1–3 and provide precise pound/kilogram targets plus exact rest intervals and tempo cues.
- I can also create a 12-week forward plan starting from after Week 3’s 1RM test, with precise progression paths (e.g., linear vs. phased) based on the Week 3 results.

  - Rows or Pendlay rows: 3x8–12
  - Face pulls or band pull-aparts: 3x15
  - Lateral raises: 2–3x12
- Lower body days:
  - Hip thrusts or glute bridges: 3x8–12
  - Romanian deadlifts or eccentric deadlift work: 3x8
  - Lunges or split squats: 3x8 per leg
  - Core (planks or Pallof presses): 3x30–45s

Cardio (introduce easy volume)
- Total cardio target: ~20–25 minutes for the week, easy to moderate (RPE 3–5)
- Distribution: 2 sessions (2x12–15 minutes or 1x20–25 minutes), optional light movement on lifting days post-workout
- Modes: cycling, walking, elliptical, incline treadmill; avoid maximal efforts

Mobility and recovery
- Daily 5–10 minutes focused on hips, thoracic spine, shoulders
- 2–3 dedicated mobility sessions per week
- Sleep target: 7–9 hours; protein intake ~1.6–2.2 g/kg/day; hydration

Nutrition targets (week 1 focus; see Week 1–3 plan for progression)
- Protein: ~1.6–2.2 g/kg/day
- Calories: maintenance to modest surplus, about +200–300 kcal/day if appetite allows
- Carbs: ~3–5 g/kg/day to support training energy
- Fats: remainder of calories, roughly 0.8–1.0 g/kg/day
- Meal distribution: 4–6 meals with 25–40 g protein per meal
- Hydration: 2.5–3.5 L/day

Readiness signals and autoregulation
- Daily checks: sleep quality, appetite, mood, fatigue (0–10)
- Morning metrics: resting HR (compared to baseline; aim for near baseline or only +0 to +3 bpm)
- In-session: main lift RPE around 6–7 on work sets; no technique degradation
- If multiple signals point toward fatigue, scale back intensity and/or volume for the following week

Week 2 (gradual progression, closer to baseline exposure)
Main lifts (slightly higher tolerance and load)
- Bench press: 4 sets x 5 reps at 65–70% 1RM (target ~65–70% of pre-illness; e.g., 65–70 kg)
- Back squat: 4 sets x 5 reps at 65–70% 1RM (target ~90–95 kg)
- Deadlift: 3 sets x 5 reps at 65–70% 1RM (target ~110–115 kg)

Rationale
- Slight load increase from Week 1 while maintaining 5-rep sets to preserve technique and recovery. Use RPE ~7 on main lifts.

Accessory blocks (progressively increasing)
- Upper body days:
  - Rows/Pulls: 3x8–12
  - Push variations: 3x8–12 (incline DB or floor press)
  - Face pulls: 3x12–15
  - Curls/Triceps: 2–3x10–12
- Lower body days:
  - Hip thrusts/glute bridges: 3x8–12
  - Romanian deadlifts: 3x6–8
  - Split squats or step-ups: 3x8 per leg
  - Core: 3x20–30s carries or anti-rotation

Cardio progression
- Total cardio target: ~25–35 minutes for the week
- Distribution: 2–3 sessions; aim to add 5–10 minutes compared to Week 1
- Intensity: maintain RPE 3–5; consider one optional light tempo day (shorter, slightly faster but still conversational pace)

Nutrition progression
- Reassess weight: aim to regain some weight toward baseline
- Maintain protein: 1.6–2.2 g/kg/day
- Calorie target: maintain +150–300 kcal/day if appetite is good; favor a slight surplus if weight remains below baseline
- Carbs: adjust to energy needs; keep training fuel high
- Hydration: 2.5–3.5 L/day

Week 3 (optimize readiness for full intensity and plan 1RM testing)
Main lifts (70–75% of baseline 1RM range; conservative but building toward baseline)
- Bench press: 4 sets x 4–5 reps at 70–75% 1RM
- Back squat: 4 sets x 4–5 reps at 70–75% 1RM
- Deadlift: 3 sets x 4–5 reps at 70–75% 1RM

1RM testing window (late Week 3)
- Plan to test bench, squat, and deadlift as a safe, non-fatiguing sequence. Recommendations:
  - Week 3 Day 4 or 3–4: bench 1RM attempts (rotate with other lifts to manage fatigue)
  - Week 3 Day 5 or 6: squat 1RM attempts
  - Week 3 Day 7: deadlift 1RM attempts
- Testing structure per lift:
  - 5–10 min warm-up ramp to working sets
  - Gradual increases: 40%, 50%, 60%, 70%, 80%, 85%, 90%, 95%, then 1RM attempts with 1–2 kg increments if form remains solid
  - Allow 3–5 minutes between attempts; ensure proper form and safe execution
- If fatigue or form breaks, stop attempts and use a lower-load maximum (e.g., 5–3–2 rep max approach) and postpone final 1RM attempts to a later date

Post-1RM plan (Week 4 onward)
- Recalculate 1RM targets based on test results
- Reset the weekly progression:
  - Example starting range: 72–78% 1RM for initial volume blocks
  - Progressive intakes: aim for steady progression with micro-load increases weekly
- If fatigue after testing, implement a brief maintenance or delayed progression block before increasing again

Daily schedule example (one possible weekly layout)
- Monday: Day A – Upper body press
  - Bench 4x5 @ 60–62.5% (Week 1) → advance to 65–70% by Week 2; 70–75% by Week 3
  - Accessory blocks
  - Optional cardio after lifting (low intensity)
- Tuesday: Day B – Lower body squat
  - Squat 4x5 @ 85 kg (Week 1) → 90–95 kg Week 2 → 95–100 kg Week 3
  - Accessory blocks

  - Cardio optional after
- Friday: Day D – Lower body hinge/accessory
  - Deadlift 3x5 @ 105 kg (Week 1) → 110–115 kg Week 2 → 115–120 kg Week 3
  - Core and mobility

Strict caveats and safety
- If any red flags appear (pain, chest tightness, fever, persistent cough, dizziness), pause and reassess with a medical professional if needed.
- Technique first: always prioritize form; if form breaks, reduce load or volume immediately.
- Use a proper warm-up and ramp protocol for each lift; ensure appropriate safety equipment and a spotter as needed.
- Hydration and nutrition should support the increased training demand, especially around Week 3 testing.
